html:
The Persian famine of 1917 to 1919 was a time of mass hunger and disease in Iran under the Qajar dynasty, at the end of the First World War.

Iran had declared itself neutral, but Russian, British and Ottoman armies fought across its land. They bought up or seized grain, and trade routes were cut. Drought brought poor harvests in 1917, and hoarding pushed bread prices out of reach. Typhus, cholera and then the 1918 influenza struck a weakened population.

The death toll is still debated. Serious estimates run from a few hundred thousand up to two million or more, and a few writers claim far higher figures. Part of the argument is political: some blame British policy above all, others point to many causes. It came less than fifty years after the famine of 1870 to 1872, and it left the Qajar state weaker still, a few years before Reza Khan seized power.
sum: The Persian famine of 1917 to 1919 was a time of mass hunger and disease in Iran under the Qajar dynasty, at the end of the First World War.
